# How this workbook works

Nothing on this page runs in the browser. **Every code block is meant to be copied
into RStudio on ERDA** (or your own computer — see the note in the
[appendix](#sec-erda)). All paths assume one folder, **`~/work/module2`**, so if you
put the Absalon files where the [file manifest](#sec-erda) says, every block runs
verbatim with no editing.

Two kinds of blocks appear:

- plain code blocks are **R** — paste them into the RStudio console (or, better,
  collect them in a script or Rmarkdown document as you go);
- blocks marked **TERMINAL** are shell commands — paste them into RStudio's
  **Terminal** tab, *not* the R console.

Some steps end with a *Your turn* question and a folded **Solution** — try it before
you unfold.

::: {.provenance}
Everything here uses the real Module 2 dataset: RNAseq of the fungal plant pathogen
*Colletotrichum fructicola* (Liang et al. 2018, *BMC Genomics* 19:557), four growth
forms with three replicates each — **CON** conidia, **APP** appressoria, **CIH**
cellophane infectious hyphae, **IL** infected apple leaf.

One caveat for Session 4: the gene sets are *keyword-derived* functional categories
built from the annotation text (all genes whose description matches
`cytochrome p450`, and so on) — not curated GO or PFAM terms, because this genome
ships no curated annotation. The enrichment *method* you practise is exactly the
real one; the categories are a stand-in.
:::

# Session 1 — Read quality control {#sec-qc}
[Monday 21-09]{.session-chip}

Before anything is mapped or counted, you have to look at the reads and decide what
to throw away. That decision is the whole point of this session — `filterAndTrim()`
is just the function that carries it out.

::: {.run-local}
**Get the data.** On Absalon, Module 2 → Exercises, download
`C_fructicola_GSE103878_small.zip` (139 MB). In the ERDA file manager, upload it into
your **`module2`** folder ([appendix](#sec-erda) if you have not made it yet) — ERDA
expands the zip automatically on upload. You now have
`~/work/module2/C_fructicola_GSE103878_small/` with 18 files — 9 samples x 2 mates
(forward `_1`, reverse `_2`).
:::

## 1.1 Look at the reads

```r
library(dada2)

path <- "~/work/module2/C_fructicola_GSE103878_small"
list.files(path)                 # you should see the 18 fastq.gz files

# Sort forward and reverse files so the two vectors stay in the same sample order
fnFs <- sort(list.files(path, pattern = "_1.fastq.gz", full.names = TRUE))
fnRs <- sort(list.files(path, pattern = "_2.fastq.gz", full.names = TRUE))

plotQualityProfile(fnFs[1:2])    # forward reads
plotQualityProfile(fnRs[1:2])    # reverse reads
```

*Question:* look at the file names first — where do these files come from, and what
does each part of a name mean?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Take `APP1small_SRR6041847_1.fastq.gz`: **APP1** = appressoria, replicate 1;
**small** = a subsample made for this course so the files stay manageable;
**SRR6041847** = the run accession in NCBI's Sequence Read Archive, where the
authors deposited the raw data (study GSE103878, Liang et al. 2018) — you could
download the full-size original from there yourself; **_1** = the forward mate of
the read pair (`_2` is the reverse); **.fastq.gz** = compressed FASTQ. Being able to
decode a sequencing file name is worth more than it looks: it is how you catch
swapped or duplicated files later.
:::

Read the plots: the grey heat map is the frequency of each quality score at each
position, the green line the median. Two features are typical of Illumina data and
both matter for what you do next: the first few cycles are noisier, and quality
decays towards the 3' end — and the **reverse reads are consistently worse** than the
forward reads, because they are sequenced last, after the cluster has degraded.

*Question:* by the way — what is the length of these reads?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**150 bp.** You can read it straight off the quality profile: the x-axis (cycle =
position in the read) runs to 150, and the sequencer produces one base per cycle.
Both mates are 150 bp, so this is $2 \times 150$ bp paired-end Illumina data. To check it
from the data rather than the plot:

```r
library(ShortRead)
fq <- readFastq(fnFs[1])
table(width(fq))          # every read: 150
```

Knowing the read length matters immediately: it is the upper bound for `truncLen`
in §1.4, and after `trimLeft = 10` your forward reads are effectively 140 bp.
:::

*Your turn:* plot a forward and a reverse profile of the **same** sample next to
each other. Which is worse, and where?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```r
plotQualityProfile(c(fnFs[1], fnRs[1]))
```
The reverse read (`_2`) sits visibly lower, and the gap widens towards the 3' end —
that is where truncation will help most.
:::

## 1.2 Expected errors — the number `maxEE` actually filters on

`filterAndTrim(maxEE = 2)` does not count bad bases. It converts each quality score
to an error probability and adds them up:

$$
P(\text{error}) = 10^{-Q/10}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
EE = \sum_{i} 10^{-Q_i/10}
$$

A read is discarded when its expected number of errors exceeds `maxEE`. Convince
yourself with ten quality scores from a real read:

```r
Q <- c(38, 38, 37, 36, 32, 30, 28, 24, 20, 15)

p_error <- 10^(-Q / 10)          # probability each base is wrong

signif(p_error, 2)
sum(p_error)                     # expected errors in these 10 bases

10^(-38/10)                      # a Q38 base is wrong ~1.6 times in 10,000
10^(-15/10)                      # a Q15 base: ~3 in 100 — worse than 100 good ones
```

Expected errors are dominated by the few worst bases — which is why trimming the
low-quality tail is so effective at rescuing reads.

## 1.3 Set up the output files

```r
# Build one clean name per sample from the file names (see §2.2 for how this works)
sample.names <- paste(sapply(strsplit(basename(fnFs), "_"), `[`, 1),
                      sapply(strsplit(basename(fnFs), "_"), `[`, 2), sep = "_")
sample.names

# Filtered files go into a filtered/ subdirectory
filtFs <- file.path(path, "filtered", paste0(sample.names, "_F_filt.fastq.gz"))
filtRs <- file.path(path, "filtered", paste0(sample.names, "_R_filt.fastq.gz"))
names(filtFs) <- sample.names
names(filtRs) <- sample.names
```

## 1.4 Choose the parameters and run the filter

The decision you are making: longer reads carry more information but accumulate more
expected errors, so retention drops. `truncLen` cuts the 3' end, `trimLeft` the noisy
first cycles, `maxEE` sets the error budget.

```r
out <- filterAndTrim(fnFs, filtFs, fnRs, filtRs,
                     trimLeft   = 10,             # drop the noisy first cycles
                     truncLen   = c(150, 125),    # forward, reverse
                     maxEE      = c(2, 2),
                     truncQ     = 2, minLen = 35, rm.phix = TRUE,
                     compress   = TRUE, multithread = FALSE)
out                                # reads.in vs reads.out per sample
round(100 * out[, "reads.out"] / out[, "reads.in"], 1)   # % kept
```

*Question (big-data aside):* what would happen if R loaded an entire FASTQ file
into memory? How does `filterAndTrim` deal with this — and if you set
`multithread = TRUE`, how many parallel threads could be started, and how does that
relate to the memory of the machine?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Our course files are subsampled, but a real FASTQ from one sample is routinely
**several gigabytes compressed** — tens of gigabytes as text. Loading a few of those
whole would exhaust the RAM of almost any machine and crash the session. dada2
avoids this by **streaming**: the file is read in chunks of a fixed number of reads,
each chunk is filtered and written out, and memory use stays constant no matter how
big the file is.

With `multithread = TRUE`, one worker can run per CPU core — on an ERDA DAG session
that is up to **8**. But each worker holds its own chunk in memory, so the real
limit is *threads x memory-per-thread must fit in the machine's RAM* (16 GB on
DAG). More threads is faster only until you hit that ceiling — which is why "just
use all the cores" is not automatically the right call on a shared machine.
:::

*Your turn:* re-run with `truncLen = c(150, 150)` (no truncation of the reverse
reads) into a **different** output folder and compare the percentages. Why does
keeping more sequence cost you reads?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```r
filtFs2 <- file.path(path, "filtered150", paste0(sample.names, "_F_filt.fastq.gz"))
filtRs2 <- file.path(path, "filtered150", paste0(sample.names, "_R_filt.fastq.gz"))
out2 <- filterAndTrim(fnFs, filtFs2, fnRs, filtRs2,
                      trimLeft = 10, truncLen = c(150, 150), maxEE = c(2, 2),
                      truncQ = 2, minLen = 35, rm.phix = TRUE,
                      compress = TRUE, multithread = FALSE)
round(100 * out2[, "reads.out"] / out2[, "reads.in"], 1)
```
Retention of the reverse reads drops by several percent: the last 25 cycles are the
worst ones, so keeping them pushes many reads over the `maxEE = 2` budget. Truncating
at 125 keeps ~95% of reverse reads; at 150 it is closer to 90%. The choice is a
trade-off you should be able to defend, not a default.
:::

# Session 2 — Read mapping and the count table {#sec-mapping}
[Wednesday 23-09]{.session-chip}

## 2.1 Run kallisto

::: {.terminal}
**kallisto runs in a terminal, not in R.** In RStudio, click the **Terminal** tab
(next to Console). From Absalon, put the `kallisto` program file and the transcripts
FASTA (`GSE103878_1104.transcripts.fasta`) directly into `~/work/module2` first.
Then paste:

```bash
cd ~/work/module2
ls -al                    # check: kallisto, the .fasta, and the reads folder
./kallisto                # prints its usage text -> the program itself works

# 1. Build the index once (takes a few minutes)
./kallisto index -i C_fructicola_GSE103878.idx GSE103878_1104.transcripts.fasta

# 2. Quantify one sample (paired-end: forward file, then reverse file)
mkdir -p results
./kallisto quant -i C_fructicola_GSE103878.idx -o results/APP1 -t 2 \
    C_fructicola_GSE103878_small/filtered/APP1small_SRR6041847_F_filt.fastq.gz \
    C_fructicola_GSE103878_small/filtered/APP1small_SRR6041847_R_filt.fastq.gz

# 3. Repeat for every sample — only the sample name changes.
#    Each run writes results/<SAMPLE>/abundance.tsv
```

The `./` in `./kallisto` means "the program file in this folder" — without it the
terminal looks for an installed program and reports `command not found`.

Useful terminal commands: `cd dirname` (enter a directory), `cd ..` (go up),
`ls -al` (list with detail), `mkdir xx` (create), `pwd` (where am I).

If your own run does not finish, Absalon has the finished output:
`abundance_files_from_kallisto.zip` — upload it to `~/work/module2` (it expands
automatically) and carry on.
:::

Watch what kallisto prints as it runs — the **pseudoalignment rate** is your first
sign of trouble. Each `abundance.tsv` has one row per transcript:

```
target_id | length | eff_length | est_counts | tpm
```

`est_counts` is the estimated reads assigned to the transcript; `eff_length` is the
length corrected for the fragment-length distribution; `tpm` is transcripts per
million — length- and depth-normalised, so it sums to 1e6 in every sample.

## 2.2 The sample-name puzzle

Before you can combine nine output files you need nine clean sample names. Work
through why each attempt fails:

```r
fnames <- c("APP1small_SRR6041847_1.fastq.gz", "APP2small_SRR6041848_1.fastq.gz",
            "CON1small_SRR6041844_1.fastq.gz", "CON2small_SRR6041845_1.fastq.gz")

# strsplit() cuts each name at every "_" and returns a LIST of pieces
strsplit(fnames, "_")[[1]]

# take the 1st and 2nd piece of each name
part1 <- sapply(strsplit(fnames, "_"), function(x) x[1])
part2 <- sapply(strsplit(fnames, "_"), function(x) x[2])
part1
part2

c(part1, part2)          # stacks them into 8 elements. No.
paste(part1, part2)      # joined with a SPACE. No.
paste0(part1, part2)     # no separator at all. No.
```

*Your turn:* produce `"APP1small_SRR6041847"` etc. — the two pieces joined with an
underscore.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```r
sample.names <- paste(part1, part2, sep = "_")
sample.names
```
`paste()` takes a `sep` argument. The `sapply`/`strsplit`/`paste` pattern is the
standard way to turn file names into sample names.
:::

## 2.3 Build the count matrix

The count table is just the `est_counts` column of every sample, glued side by side
and keyed on `target_id`. Base R does it in a few lines — here from the backup
folder, which everyone has; if you use your own `results/`, only the two
`list.files()` lines change:

```r
abdir <- "~/work/module2/abundance_files_from_kallisto"
files <- list.files(abdir, pattern = "_abundance.tsv$", full.names = TRUE)
samps <- sub("_abundance.tsv$", "", basename(files))
samps

tables <- lapply(files, read.delim)
names(tables) <- samps

# Every file must list the same transcripts in the same order — CHECK, don't assume
gene_ids <- tables[[1]]$target_id
all(sapply(tables, function(x) identical(x$target_id, gene_ids)))

count_matrix <- sapply(tables, function(x) x$est_counts)
rownames(count_matrix) <- gene_ids
dim(count_matrix)
round(head(count_matrix, 4))
```

`est_counts` — not `tpm` — is the column DESeq2 needs. TPM has already had library
size divided out; that is convenient for eyeballing expression, but it destroys the
information DESeq2 needs, namely **how many reads** a measurement is based on. A gene
at 50 TPM in a 40-million-read sample is far more reliable than the same 50 TPM in a
2-million-read one, and only the raw counts still know the difference.

```r
colSums(count_matrix)                                   # depth differs a lot
tpm_matrix <- sapply(tables, function(x) x$tpm)
round(colSums(tpm_matrix))                              # 1e6 everywhere, by design
```

## 2.4 Check the matrix before you trust it

Never hand a count matrix to DESeq2 without looking at it. The cheapest check is
whether any two columns are identical — biological replicates never are.

```r
round(cor(log2(count_matrix + 1)), 3)          # anything EXACTLY 1 off-diagonal?

which(duplicated(t(count_matrix)))             # any column an exact copy?

# the smoking gun, at file level:
tools::md5sum(file.path(abdir, c("CON1_abundance.tsv", "CON2_abundance.tsv")))
```

::: {.provenance}
You will find that **CON1 and CON2 are byte-identical** — the same file twice, with
a correlation of exactly 1. Two biological replicates cannot be identical to the last
decimal, so this is a file-handling mistake in the course archive, not biology. Had
you run DESeq2 on this matrix it would have reported an impossibly small within-group
variance for CON and inflated your significance. **This is why you look first.**
(The main count table used in Session 3 is unaffected — its CON1 and CON2 are
genuinely different.)
:::

# Session 3 — Differential expression {#sec-de}
[Monday 28-09 · Wednesday 30-09]{.session-chip}

From here on we use the **full** course count matrix — all 12 samples including the
infected leaf (IL), all 17,827 genes, mapped with Bowtie2 and counted with HTSeq as
described in Liang et al. 2018.

::: {.run-local}
**Get the data.** From Absalon, upload `C_fructicola_counts.zip` into
`~/work/module2` — it expands automatically, giving you
`~/work/module2/C_fructicola_counts/` with the count table and the annotation.
:::

## 3.1 Load the counts and build the DESeq2 object

```r
library(DESeq2)

countdata <- read.delim("~/work/module2/C_fructicola_counts/GSE103878_1104.genes.count.txt",
                        row.names = 1)
dim(countdata)
head(countdata, 3)

# the condition of each sample, read straight off the column names
coldata <- data.frame(
  row.names = colnames(countdata),
  condition = factor(sub("[0-9]+$", "", colnames(countdata)))
)
coldata

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = countdata,
                              colData   = coldata,
                              design    = ~ condition)

dds <- dds[rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10, ]     # prefilter: drop genes with <10 reads total
dds
```

Why prefilter? Genes with almost no reads cannot give a reliable fold change, they
inflate the multiple-testing burden (§3.8), and dropping them costs nothing.

## 3.2 Library size, and a first look at IL

```r
depth <- colSums(countdata)
cond_col <- c(CON = "#4C72B0", APP = "#DD8452", CIH = "#55A868", IL = "#C44E52")
barplot(depth / 1e6, las = 2, ylab = "Million mapped reads",
        col = cond_col[as.character(coldata$condition)],   # as.character: a factor
        main = "Library size per sample")                  # would index by level number
```

The three IL samples are dramatically smaller. Hold that thought — §3.3 explains it.

## 3.3 Size factors: run DESeq2, then beat it by hand

```r
dds <- DESeq(dds)          # size factors + dispersions + Wald test, in one call
sizeFactors(dds)
```

This is the single most useful thing to understand about DESeq2, and it is five
lines of base R. DESeq2 does **not** normalise by total reads (one runaway gene
would drag every other gene down). It uses the **median-of-ratios**: for each gene,
compute its geometric mean across samples (a synthetic reference sample); divide
each sample's counts by that reference; the sample's size factor is the **median**
of those ratios — and a median cannot be moved by a handful of extreme genes.

*Your turn:* implement it and compare with `sizeFactors(dds)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```r
log_cnt <- log(as.matrix(countdata))    # log of every count; zeros become -Inf
ref     <- rowMeans(log_cnt)            # log geometric mean per gene
keep    <- is.finite(ref)               # drop genes with a zero in ANY sample
ratios  <- log_cnt[keep, ] - ref[keep]
my_sf   <- exp(apply(ratios, 2, median))

round(cbind(mine = my_sf, DESeq2 = sizeFactors(dds)), 4)
```
They match to four decimals. (Median, not mean — the whole point is robustness to
outliers.)
:::

Now look at what you computed:

```r
round(sort(sizeFactors(dds)), 3)
```

The IL size factors are roughly **0.10–0.27** against ~2.5 for APP — an order of
magnitude. The reason is biological, not technical: IL is RNA extracted from an
*infected apple leaf*, so most of the RNA in the tube is **apple**, not fungus. Only
a small fraction of reads maps to the *C. fructicola* transcriptome, so the fungal
library is effectively tiny. This is exactly what size factors are for — but it also
means IL carries much less statistical power.

## 3.4 Variance stabilisation, PCA and sample distances

Raw RNAseq counts are heteroscedastic: highly expressed genes vary more in absolute
terms. `vst()` corrects this, and PCA and clustering are run on VST values, never on
raw counts.

```r
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)

# mean-SD before and after: a flat trend is the goal
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
lc <- log2(counts(dds) + 1)
plot(rowMeans(lc), apply(lc, 1, sd), pch = 20, cex = 0.3,
     col = adjustcolor("grey30", 0.25),
     xlab = "mean log2(count+1)", ylab = "SD", main = "log2(count + 1)")
lines(lowess(rowMeans(lc), apply(lc, 1, sd)), col = "red", lwd = 2.5)
va <- assay(vsd)
plot(rowMeans(va), apply(va, 1, sd), pch = 20, cex = 0.3,
     col = adjustcolor("grey30", 0.25),
     xlab = "mean VST value", ylab = "SD", main = "vst()")
lines(lowess(rowMeans(va), apply(va, 1, sd)), col = "red", lwd = 2.5)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# PCA — replicates should group, conditions should separate
plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = "condition")

# sample-to-sample distances
d <- dist(t(assay(vsd)))
plot(hclust(d), labels = colnames(vsd), main = "Sample clustering", xlab = "", sub = "")

# dispersion estimates — the model DESeq2 fitted
plotDispEsts(dds)
```

The PCA axes show percentages of variance; they do not add to 100% because there are
as many components as samples minus one — PC1 and PC2 are simply the two directions
capturing the most.

## 3.5 The results table

```r
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "APP", "CON"), alpha = 0.05)
summary(res)
head(res[order(res$padj), ])

sum(res$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)                            # significant genes
sum(res$padj < 0.05 & res$log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE)   # up in APP
sum(is.na(res$padj))                # removed by independent filtering — that is normal
```

*Question:* re-run `results()` **without** `alpha = 0.05` (the default is 0.1). How
many genes are significantly up-regulated now, and why does the number change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```r
res10 <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "APP", "CON"))   # default alpha = 0.1
summary(res10)
sum(res10$padj < 0.1, na.rm = TRUE)
```
More genes pass. Two things moved at once: the reporting threshold itself
(padj < 0.1 instead of < 0.05), and DESeq2's **independent filtering**, which is
optimised *for the alpha you declare* — so even the padj values themselves can
differ slightly between the two runs. The practical lesson: `alpha` is part of your
method, so state it in your report, and set it to the threshold you actually intend
to use.
:::

## 3.6 MA plot and volcano plot

```r
plotMA(res, ylim = c(-12, 12))

# volcano, by hand
sig <- !is.na(res$padj) & res$padj < 0.05
plot(res$log2FoldChange, -log10(res$pvalue), pch = 20, cex = 0.35,
     col = ifelse(sig, adjustcolor("#C44E52", 0.55), adjustcolor("grey40", 0.35)),
     xlab = "log2 fold change (APP / CON)", ylab = "-log10(p-value)",
     main = "Volcano plot", xlim = c(-12, 12))
abline(v = c(-1, 1), lty = 2, col = "grey40")
```

Low-expression genes fan out on the left of the MA plot: with few reads the fold
change is poorly determined — exactly why the prefilter and DESeq2's independent
filtering exist.

## 3.7 Annotate and save

```r
annot <- read.delim("~/work/module2/C_fructicola_counts/GSE103878_1104_genes_annot.tab")
out   <- merge(as.data.frame(res), annot, by.x = "row.names", by.y = "ID", all.x = TRUE)

# the 10 most strongly up-regulated genes in appressoria, with their function
up <- out[!is.na(out$padj) & out$padj < 0.05 & out$log2FoldChange > 0, ]
head(up[order(-up$log2FoldChange), c("Row.names", "log2FoldChange", "padj", "Annotation")], 10)

write.csv(out, "~/work/module2/DE_APP_vs_CON.csv")   # saved under ~/work = kept
```

*Question:* which column of the results table should you use to find the "most
differentially expressed" genes — and what do its values actually mean?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For *most changed in expression*, rank on **`log2FoldChange`**: it is the effect
size on a $\log_2$ scale, so $+2$ means $2^2 = 4\times$ higher in APP than CON and
$-3$ means $2^3 = 8\times$ lower.
`padj` answers a different question — how strong the *evidence* is, not how big the
change is: a gene can have a tiny fold change with a minuscule padj just because it
is measured very precisely. Report both. For ranking by fold change specifically,
DESeq2's `lfcShrink()` gives *shrunken* estimates that stop lowly-expressed, noisy
genes from topping the list with huge but meaningless fold changes.
:::

Most of the extreme fold changes belong to hypothetical proteins — normal for a
fungal genome, and a reminder that a big log2FC is not the same as an interpretable
result.

*Your turn:* plot the normalised counts of the single most strongly up-regulated
gene across all four conditions. How is it expressed in CIH and IL?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```r
top_gene <- up$Row.names[which.max(up$log2FoldChange)]
plotCounts(dds, gene = top_gene, intgroup = "condition")
annot$Annotation[annot$ID == top_gene]
```
:::

## 3.8 Multiple testing

14,000 tests at p < 0.05 would give ~700 false positives by chance alone. That is
what the adjusted p-value fixes:

```r
p <- res$pvalue[!is.na(res$pvalue)]

sum(p < 0.05)                                    # raw hits
sum(p.adjust(p, method = "bonferroni") < 0.05)   # controls ANY false positive: harsh
sum(p.adjust(p, method = "BH") < 0.05)           # controls the false discovery rate
round(0.05 * length(p))                          # expected false positives among raw hits
```

Bonferroni controls the probability of even *one* false positive and is very
conservative; Benjamini–Hochberg controls the *fraction* of false positives among
the genes you call significant (the FDR) — the right trade-off when screening
thousands of genes. `padj` in a DESeq2 table is BH.

## 3.9 Comparing two contrasts

`results()` can extract any pair. Comparing two contrasts separates genes specific
to appressoria from the general infection programme:

```r
res_cih <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "CIH", "CON"), alpha = 0.05)

m <- merge(as.data.frame(res)[, c("log2FoldChange", "padj")],
           as.data.frame(res_cih)[, c("log2FoldChange", "padj")],
           by = "row.names", suffixes = c("_APP", "_CIH"))
m <- m[!is.na(m$padj_APP) & !is.na(m$padj_CIH), ]

plot(m$log2FoldChange_APP, m$log2FoldChange_CIH, pch = 20, cex = 0.3,
     col = adjustcolor("grey30", 0.3),
     xlab = "log2FC APP vs CON", ylab = "log2FC CIH vs CON")
abline(0, 1, col = "blue", lty = 2); abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "grey60", lty = 3)
cor(m$log2FoldChange_APP, m$log2FoldChange_CIH)

# up in APP but NOT in CIH — candidate appressorium-specific genes
app_only <- m$Row.names[m$padj_APP < 0.05 & m$log2FoldChange_APP > 2 &
                        (m$padj_CIH >= 0.05 | abs(m$log2FoldChange_CIH) < 1)]
length(app_only)
```

# Session 4 — Enrichment and clustering {#sec-enrich}
[Wednesday 30-09 afternoon]{.session-chip}

You now have thousands of significant genes, which is not an answer to a biological
question. Enrichment analysis turns that list into statements about **function**.
This whole session is base R — `phyper`, `fisher.test`, `p.adjust`, `kmeans` — run
on the objects you built in Session 3.

::: {.run-local}
**One extra file.** The functional categories for this genome are in
`gene_sets.csv`. Fetch it straight into `module2` from the R console:

```r
download.file("https://mutwil.github.io/bigdata-module2-transcriptomics/data/gene_sets.csv",
              "~/work/module2/gene_sets.csv")
```

(It is also fine to download it in a browser from that address and upload it.)
:::

## 4.1 The gene list, the universe, and the sets

```r
gene_sets <- read.csv("~/work/module2/gene_sets.csv")
head(gene_sets, 3)
sort(table(gene_sets$term_name), decreasing = TRUE)

universe <- rownames(res)[!is.na(res$padj)]    # every gene actually tested
de_genes <- rownames(res)[!is.na(res$padj) & res$padj < 0.05 & res$log2FoldChange > 2]
length(universe); length(de_genes)
```

The threshold (`log2FC > 2`) is a **choice you are making** — §4.6 shows how much it
matters.

## 4.2 The hypergeometric test, by hand

The lecture's question — *is the overlap larger than expected by random sampling?* —
is answered by the hypergeometric distribution. Four numbers define it: $N$ the
universe, $n$ your DE list, $K$ the genes of the set inside the universe, $k$ the
overlap. The p-value is the probability of an overlap at least as large by chance:

$$
P(X \ge k) \;=\; \sum_{j=k}^{\min(n,\,K)}
\frac{\binom{K}{j}\binom{N-K}{\,n-j\,}}{\binom{N}{n}}
$$

which is exactly what `phyper()` computes.

```r
set_genes <- gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == "Cytochrome P450"]

N <- length(universe)
n <- length(de_genes)
K <- sum(set_genes %in% universe)
k <- sum(de_genes %in% set_genes)
c(N = N, n = n, K = K, k = k)

n * K / N                        # expected overlap by chance
k / (n * K / N)                  # fold enrichment (~1 = exactly what chance predicts)

# P(X >= k): phyper gives P(X <= q), so ask for the upper tail at k - 1
phyper(k - 1, K, N - K, n, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

Beware the off-by-one: passing `k` instead of `k - 1` silently makes every p-value
too small, because "at least k" must include k itself.

```r
# Fisher's exact test on the 2x2 table is the identical calculation
tab <- matrix(c(k, n - k, K - k, N - n - (K - k)), nrow = 2)
fisher.test(tab, alternative = "greater")$p.value
```

## 4.3 Does your code actually work? Use a positive control

Cytochrome P450 comes out at fold ≈ 1 — no enrichment. Before concluding anything
biological, rule out the other explanation: that your code is wrong. Build a gene
list you *know* is enriched:

```r
set.seed(1)
p450 <- intersect(gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == "Cytochrome P450"], universe)
fake <- c(sample(p450, 60), sample(setdiff(universe, p450), 240))

kf <- sum(fake %in% p450); Kf <- length(p450); nf <- length(fake)
kf / (nf * Kf / N)                                    # fold enrichment ~15
phyper(kf - 1, Kf, N - Kf, nf, lower.tail = FALSE)    # astronomically small
```

The machinery works. So when the real data gives nothing, that is a statement about
the data, not a bug.

## 4.4 Test every category

```r
res_enrich <- data.frame()
for (tm in unique(gene_sets$term_name)) {
  sg <- gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == tm]
  K  <- sum(sg %in% universe)
  k  <- sum(de_genes %in% sg)
  if (K < 5) next
  res_enrich <- rbind(res_enrich, data.frame(
    term = tm, set_size = K, overlap = k,
    expected = round(n * K / N, 2),
    fold     = round(k / (n * K / N), 2),
    pvalue   = phyper(k - 1, K, N - K, n, lower.tail = FALSE)))
}
res_enrich$padj <- p.adjust(res_enrich$pvalue, method = "BH")   # same issue as §3.8!
res_enrich <- res_enrich[order(res_enrich$pvalue), ]

head(res_enrich, 12)
sum(res_enrich$pvalue < 0.05)      # raw
sum(res_enrich$padj  < 0.05)       # after BH
```

## 4.5 Nothing is significant. Why?

This is the most common outcome of a first real enrichment analysis, and being able
to diagnose it is worth more than a lucky hit. Four things work against us here, and
you can check each one:

1. **The gene list is enormous** — ~18% of all tested genes. A list that big
   overlaps every category at roughly the background rate; enrichment needs a
   *selective* list.
2. **The categories are protein families, not biological processes.** "Protein
   kinase" is scattered across every pathway; real GO terms describe processes
   switched on together — a family has no reason to move as a block.
3. **BH still costs us** even with only ~29 categories — check the gap between the
   best raw p-value and its padj.
4. **Most of the genome has no usable annotation** — count how many of the tested
   genes appear in no category at all (`sum(!(universe %in% gene_sets$gene))`);
   they can never contribute a hit.

It would be easy to make this session produce an impressive table by hunting for a
category and threshold that happen to pass. That is p-hacking, and it is the single
most common way enrichment analysis is abused in the literature. The result above is
what this data honestly gives.

## 4.6 How much does the threshold matter?

```r
for (lfc in c(1, 2, 3)) {
  dg <- rownames(res)[!is.na(res$padj) & res$padj < 0.05 & res$log2FoldChange > lfc]
  out <- data.frame()
  for (tm in unique(gene_sets$term_name)) {
    sg <- gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == tm]
    K  <- sum(sg %in% universe); k <- sum(dg %in% sg)
    if (K < 5) next
    out <- rbind(out, data.frame(term = tm,
                 p = phyper(k - 1, K, N - K, length(dg), lower.tail = FALSE)))
  }
  out <- out[order(out$p), ]
  cat(sprintf("log2FC > %d (%5d genes): best raw p = %.3f | top 3: %s\n",
              lfc, length(dg), min(out$p), paste(head(out$term, 3), collapse = " | ")))
}
```

The ranking reshuffles as the threshold moves — a different cut-off would have given
you a different "top hit" to write about. This is exactly the lecture's argument for
**whole-distribution methods**: GSEA ranks *every* gene and asks where a set's
members fall in that ranking, with no threshold at all. With curated annotation you
would run it with `fgsea` or `clusterProfiler`; for this genome, GO or PFAM terms
would first have to come from InterProScan or eggNOG-mapper.

## 4.7 Clustering expression profiles

Enrichment on one gene list answers one question. Clustering first, then testing
each cluster, asks *which programmes* the fungus runs in *which* growth form — the
analysis on the last slide of the lecture.

```r
conds <- c("CON", "APP", "CIH", "IL")
va    <- assay(vsd)
prof  <- sapply(conds, function(cd) rowMeans(va[, coldata$condition == cd]))

# genes that actually change, scaled to shape rather than level
vary   <- names(sort(apply(prof, 1, var), decreasing = TRUE))[1:1500]
scaled <- t(scale(t(prof[vary, ])))

set.seed(42)
km <- kmeans(scaled, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
table(km$cluster)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (i in 1:4) {
  members <- scaled[km$cluster == i, ]
  matplot(t(members[1:min(120, nrow(members)), ]), type = "l", lty = 1,
          col = adjustcolor("grey50", 0.25), xaxt = "n",
          ylab = "scaled expression",
          main = paste0("Cluster ", i, " (n = ", sum(km$cluster == i), ")"))
  lines(km$centers[i, ], col = "#C44E52", lwd = 3)
  axis(1, 1:4, conds)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

*Your turn:* run the §4.4 loop on one cluster's genes, with the 1,500 variable genes
as the universe. Do the CON-peaking cluster's top categories make biological sense?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```r
i  <- which.max(km$centers[, "CON"])          # the CON-peaking cluster
cl <- rownames(scaled)[km$cluster == i]
Nu <- length(vary); nn <- length(cl)
out <- data.frame()
for (tm in unique(gene_sets$term_name)) {
  sg <- gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == tm]
  K  <- sum(sg %in% vary); k <- sum(cl %in% sg)
  if (K < 5) next
  out <- rbind(out, data.frame(term = tm, overlap = k, set_size = K,
               fold = round(k / (nn * K / Nu), 2),
               p = phyper(k - 1, K, Nu - K, nn, lower.tail = FALSE)))
}
out$padj <- p.adjust(out$p, "BH")
head(out[order(out$p), ], 5)
```
A cluster is a much more coherent list than "everything with padj < 0.05" — the
folds rise, and the CON cluster leans towards cytochrome P450 and
heterokaryon-incompatibility genes (raw p ≈ 0.015). But nothing survives BH, so the
honest way to report it is as a hypothesis, never as a finding.
:::

# Appendix — Connecting to RStudio on ERDA {#sec-erda}

Everything in this module runs in RStudio on ERDA. This is how you get there.
**Do the sign-up before the first class** — it is not instant.

## 1. Get an ERDA account

ERDA is the University of Copenhagen's *Electronic Research Data Archive*. Go to
[erda.dk](https://erda.dk) and choose **"Sign up to ERDA using your KU / UCPH
account"**, then log in with your usual KU credentials. ERDA supports two-factor
authentication, so have your phone to hand.

You only need a web browser. Nothing is installed on your own machine.

## 2. Start an RStudio session

Once you are logged in to ERDA (follow along in the **R Studio on ERDA** slides in
the *General course information* module on Absalon — they show a screenshot of every
step):

1. On the ERDA home page, click the **Jupyter** app (also in the left icon bar).
2. Under **Select a Jupyter Service**, stay on the **DAG** tab (*Data Analysis
   Gateway* — the interactive service; MODI is for batch HPC jobs) and press
   **Start DAG**.
3. You land on **JupyterHub**. Press **Start My Server**.
4. Under **Server Options → Select a notebook image**, choose
   **Big Data in Biotechnology Notebook** — this is the course's own image with the
   right packages preinstalled. Do not take the default Python notebook.
5. When the launcher opens, click **RStudio** (under *Notebook*). The same launcher
   also offers **Terminal** under *Other*.

You now have RStudio running in your browser on a KU machine. Worth knowing about
DAG sessions: you get **8 cores and 16 GB of memory**, a session is **terminated
after 2 hours of inactivity**, and the machine itself is **non-persistent** — see
the next point.

## 3. One-time setup: the `module2` folder

Your ERDA files appear inside every session at `~/work` (in full:
`/home/jovyan/work/`). **Everything in this module lives in one folder inside it.**
Make it once — paste into the RStudio console:

```r
dir.create("~/work/module2", showWarnings = FALSE)
```

(Or in the ERDA file manager: right-click → New Folder → `module2`.)

That one folder is the whole convention. Every code block on this page reads and
writes `~/work/module2/...`, so once the files below are in place, every block runs
by copy-paste alone.

::: {.provenance}
**Only `~/work` survives.** In ERDA's own words, spawned instances are
non-persistent: *any change made during a session is lost once the server is
terminated — the only exception is data saved in the provided mount directory
(`~/work`)*. And sessions do terminate: after 2 hours of inactivity, automatically.
Save everything under `~/work/module2` and it is there next session.
:::

## 4. The files: Absalon → ERDA

Everything comes from **Absalon → Module 2 — Transcriptomics**. Download from
Absalon to your computer, then upload into `~/work/module2` in the ERDA file
manager — **zips expand automatically on upload**, so there is nothing further to
do. (If a zip ever does arrive unexpanded, right-click it → Unpack.) This table is
the complete list:

| Get from Absalon | Put in ERDA | Used in |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `C_fructicola_GSE103878_small.zip` (139 MB) | upload to `module2` → expands to `C_fructicola_GSE103878_small/` | Session 1–2 |
| `kallisto` (the program file) | straight into `module2` | Session 2 |
| `GSE103878_1104.transcripts.fasta` | straight into `module2` | Session 2 |
| `abundance_files_from_kallisto.zip` | upload to `module2` → expands | Session 2 |
| `C_fructicola_counts.zip` | upload to `module2` → expands to `C_fructicola_counts/` | Session 3 |
| `gene_sets.csv` — or `download.file()` as in [§4](#sec-enrich) | straight into `module2` | Session 4 |
| `CountTable_GroupExercise2025.csv` | straight into `module2` | Assignment |
| `Annot_GroupExercise2025.csv` | straight into `module2` | Assignment |

When it is all in place, `~/work/module2` looks like this:

```

    kallisto                         the program (Session 2)

```

## 5. Find the terminal — you need it for kallisto

Session 2 runs `kallisto` from a command line, not from R. You do not need to leave
RStudio:

> In RStudio, select the **Terminal** tab, immediately to the right of the
> **Console** tab in the lower-left pane.

That gives you a real shell on your ERDA virtual machine. Alternatively, go back to
the DAG launcher and choose **Terminal** instead of RStudio.

## 6. Packages

The **Big Data in Biotechnology Notebook** image already has the packages this
course needs, including `dada2`, `DESeq2` and the tidyverse — that is the point of
picking it in step 2. On ERDA, **you never install anything.** If a package seems
missing, first check you selected the course image rather than the default one, and
otherwise tell a teacher.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Working on your own computer instead"}
Allowed, but you take on the setup yourself. Install
[R](https://cran.r-project.org/) and
[RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/), then the packages:

```r
install.packages("tidyverse")
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install(c("dada2", "DESeq2"))
```

`kallisto` needs the binary for your operating system from the
[kallisto download page](https://pachterlab.github.io/kallisto/download) (the copy
on Absalon is the **Linux** build, for ERDA — it will not run on macOS or Windows).
Use a folder of your choosing instead of `~/work/module2` and adjust the paths at
the top of each block, but keep the same layout. The teachers can only reliably
help with the ERDA setup.
:::

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | What to do |
|:--|:--|
| Session will not start, or times out | Wait and try again; a stuck session usually clears. Note sessions end after 2 h of inactivity. |
| R packages missing (`library(dada2)` fails) | You started the wrong notebook image. Stop the server (JupyterHub → Home) and start it again with **Big Data in Biotechnology Notebook**. |
| Cannot see your files in RStudio | You are probably not under `~/work`. Run `getwd()`; the module folder is `~/work/module2`. |
| Work disappeared after a session ended | Only `~/work` persists. Anything saved elsewhere was on the temporary machine. |
| `kallisto: command not found` | You are missing the `./` — the program is a file in your folder, so run `./kallisto`. |
| A path from this page does not exist | A file from the §4 table is missing, or a zip expanded into an extra nesting level — check `~/work/module2` against the layout above. (The exercise HTMLs on Absalon use the author's own paths; the ones on this page are the canonical ones.) |
| Everything is slow | Big files (the 139 MB read set) take time to upload and expand. This is normal. |

If ERDA itself is broken rather than your code, mail **support@erda.dk** — they
usually reply within one working day.
